body:
Karnataka as an important centre of Jainism

Karnataka became one of the important regions of Jain religious activity in southern India. Jain teachers and monastic communities were supported by lay followers, local ruling families and influential ministers.

The region is especially associated with the Digambara Jain tradition, although its history includes different Jain communities and forms of patronage.

Three associations are particularly useful for preliminary study: the tradition of Chandragupta Maurya and Bhadrabahu at Shravanabelagola, the patronage of the Rashtrakutas, and the monument commissioned by Chamundaraya under the Western Ganga rulers.

Shravanabelagola and its 2 hills

Shravanabelagola is an important Jain pilgrimage centre in Hassan district, Karnataka. It lies between 2 notable hills: Chandragiri and Vindhyagiri.

Chandragiri

Chandragiri is associated with the Jain traditions concerning Bhadrabahu and Chandragupta Maurya. It contains Jain religious buildings and memorials connected with monastic history. The association of Chandragupta with this site belongs to the traditional account of his renunciation and migration south.

Vindhyagiri

Vindhyagiri is famous for the large monolithic statue of Gomateshwara, or Bahubali. A monolithic statue is carved from a single mass of stone.

The statue was commissioned in 981 CE by Chamundaraya, also written Chavundaraya, a powerful minister and military commander associated with the Western Ganga dynasty.

Bahubali is a revered figure in Jain tradition. The statue represents his renunciation and spiritual discipline. Bahubali and Mahavira are not the same person.

Royal and ministerial patronage

The Western Ganga rulers were important supporters of Jain institutions in Karnataka. Chamundaraya's commission of the Gomateshwara statue demonstrates that influential ministers, not only kings, could become major patrons of religious activity.

The Rashtrakuta dynasty also contributed to the development of Jainism in the Deccan. Amoghavarsha I, a prominent Rashtrakuta ruler of the 9th century CE, is associated with patronage of Jain learning and religious traditions.

The Jain scholar Jinasena was associated with the intellectual environment of Amoghavarsha's reign. Such associations show how support from a royal court could encourage the work of Jain scholars and teachers. Amoghavarsha's Jain connections should not be taken to mean that he supported no other religious traditions.

What Karnataka illustrates

The history of Jainism in Karnataka demonstrates several distinct forms of support. Travelling ascetics helped establish religious traditions; rulers supported Jain communities; ministers commissioned monuments; and centres such as Shravanabelagola became enduring places of pilgrimage.

Prelims focus

  • Shravanabelagola is in Hassan district, Karnataka.
  • Chandragiri is associated with Bhadrabahu and Chandragupta Maurya in Jain tradition.
  • Vindhyagiri is the site of the Gomateshwara statue.
  • Gomateshwara represents Bahubali.
  • Chamundaraya, a Western Ganga minister, commissioned the statue in 981 CE.
  • Trap: Chamundaraya commissioned the statue; it was not commissioned by Chandragupta Maurya.

[Sources: NCERT, An Introduction to Indian Art, Part I, Class 11, chapter 6, Temple Architecture and Sculpture, printed p. 94; Government of Karnataka, Karnataka Tourism, Shravanabelagola and Gommateshwara Monolith, consulted 18 November 2026; Hassan District Administration, Shravanabelgola, consulted 18 November 2026; IGNOU, History of India from c. 300 to 1206, unit Emergence of Rashtrakutas, section on Amoghavarsha I and Jain patronage.]

pictures.alt: Chandragiri links to Bhadrabahu and Chandragupta Maurya in Jain tradition; Vindhyagiri has the Bahubali statue commissioned by Chamundaraya in 981 CE.

title: The Spread of Jainism in Karnataka

body:
Gujarat as a centre of Jain learning and patronage

Gujarat became an important centre of Jainism through the combined influence of religious teachers, merchant communities, political patrons and religious institutions.

The region is particularly associated with the Svetambara Jain tradition. Its history illustrates how a religious community could expand through teaching, the preservation of texts, donations and support from ruling families.

Valabhi and early Jain learning

Valabhi, in the Saurashtra region of Gujarat, became an important centre for the preservation of Jain teachings. It is remembered for the major council associated with Devardhigani Kshamashramana, at which the surviving Svetambara scriptures were collected in written form around the 5th to early 6th century CE.

This association gives Valabhi a distinct place in Jain history. Its principal significance in this topic is the preservation of sacred texts, rather than a particular king's military achievements.

Other evidence of Jain religious activity in Gujarat includes the Jain bronze images from Akota, near Vadodara, associated with the period from about the late 5th to 7th century CE. These are a useful place-and-period association showing that Jain religious traditions had an established presence in the region.

Hemachandra and the Chaulukya rulers

During the medieval period, the Chaulukya dynasty, also called the Solanki dynasty, ruled important parts of Gujarat from its capital at Anahilavada, or Patan.

The Jain scholar and religious teacher Hemachandra became an influential figure in this political and intellectual environment. He was associated with the court of Jayasimha Siddharaja and subsequently with that of Kumarapala.

Kumarapala's patronage

Kumarapala was a Chaulukya ruler of Gujarat in the 12th century CE, generally dated to approximately 1143–1174 CE. He is especially remembered for his association with Hemachandra and for supporting Jain religious activities.

Jain accounts describe Hemachandra as having a major influence on Kumarapala's religious outlook. They also credit Kumarapala with encouraging non-violence, restricting animal killing and supporting Jain temples and institutions.

Accounts differ on the precise nature and extent of Kumarapala's personal conversion to Jainism. The important historical distinction is that his association with Hemachandra and his patronage of Jain institutions are well established, whereas every detail of the conversion narratives and reported restrictions should not be treated as equally certain.

Kumarapala–Hemachandra–Patan: Kumarapala was the ruler, Hemachandra was the Jain scholar, and Patan was the Chaulukya capital. These 3 associations belong together.

Other donors and important Jain centres

Ministers and wealthy patrons

Vimal Shah, a minister associated with the Chaulukya political world, commissioned the Vimala Vasahi Jain temple at Mount Abu in the 11th century CE.

In the 13th century CE, the brothers Vastupala and Tejapala, influential ministers associated with the Vaghela rulers of Gujarat, became prominent patrons of Jain religious buildings. Tejapala is particularly associated with the Luna Vasahi temple at Mount Abu.

These examples demonstrate that ministers and wealthy individuals could continue to support Jain institutions even beyond the reign of a particular king.

Pilgrimage centres and their locations

  • Shatrunjaya Hills near Palitana: A major Jain pilgrimage centre in the Bhavnagar region of Gujarat, known for its numerous Jain temples.
  • Girnar near Junagadh: An important Jain sacred hill in Gujarat, associated in Jain tradition with the Tirthankara Neminatha.
  • Mount Abu: The location of the famous Dilwara Jain temples, including Vimala Vasahi and Luna Vasahi. Mount Abu is in Rajasthan, not Gujarat.
  • Valabhi: The Gujarat centre associated with the preservation and redaction of Svetambara scriptures.

Connecting the major patrons and places

The main associations can be placed in a broad chronological sequence. The Mauryan period provides the traditional link between Chandragupta Maurya, Bhadrabahu and Karnataka, as well as the account of Samprati's Jain patronage. In ancient Kalinga, Kharavela is associated with the Jain caves at Udayagiri and Khandagiri.

The early medieval period is important for the Valabhi council in Gujarat. Later, Karnataka provides the example of Chamundaraya's commission in 981 CE, while Gujarat provides the example of Kumarapala and Hemachandra in the 12th century CE.

Prelims focus

  • Valabhi in Gujarat is associated with Devardhigani and the Svetambara scriptures.
  • Hemachandra was associated with Jayasimha Siddharaja and Kumarapala.
  • Kumarapala was a 12th-century Chaulukya ruler of Gujarat.
  • Anahilavada, or Patan, was the Chaulukya capital.
  • Palitana and Girnar are major Jain pilgrimage centres in Gujarat.
  • Trap: The Dilwara temples at Mount Abu are in Rajasthan, although several of their prominent patrons were connected with Gujarat.

[Sources: NCERT, Our Pasts–I, Class 6, chapter 7, New Questions and Ideas, printed p. 70; NCERT, An Introduction to Indian Art, Part I, Class 11, chapter 6, Temple Architecture and Sculpture, printed pp. 94–95; Nalini Balbir, Jainpedia, Sacred writings, section Svetambara canon, consulted 18 November 2026; Archaeological Survey of India historical volume, Kumarapala, hosted by Indira Gandhi National Centre for the Arts, printed p. 389; Samira Sheikh, State and Society in Gujarat, c. 1200–1500: The Making of a Region, Oxford doctoral thesis, discussion of Hemachandra and Chaulukya-Vaghela patronage; University of Notre Dame, Marble photographic archive, Dilwara Temple Complex: Luna Vasahi Temple, architectural history, consulted 18 November 2026.]

pictures.alt: A chronological timeline links Jain patrons and scripture redaction with their periods and regions, followed by other centres in Gujarat and Rajasthan.
pictures.caption: The main Jain patrons, councils and regional centres can be distinguished by period and place.

title: Jainism in Gujarat: Valabhi, Kumarapala and Major Centres
